title: First Rule of Entrepreneurship: There Are No Rules

canonicalEdition.name: First edition
canonicalEdition.sourceProvenance: Frozen web bundle only: bibliographic records, table-of-contents evidence, official publication metadata, and narrow secondary summary support. Paraphrase-first; no full text frozen.

anchorSummary: This chapter attacks formula thinking directly, arguing that startup leadership is dominated by paradoxes and context, so leaders need judgment strong enough to work without a comforting universal rule.
coreClaim: Entrepreneurship resists universal rules because leaders constantly face tradeoffs that only make sense in context, not in abstract best-practice slogans.
distinctMechanism: Horowitz uses acquisition pressure, accountability-versus-creativity tension, and people-management paradoxes to argue that judgment beats rigid adherence to generic rules.
requiredAnchors: Deals and operating outcomes remain contingent deep into the process, so certainty is fragile.
Accountability versus creativity is a live paradox, not a rule with a clean permanent answer.
The chapter broadens the book's anti-formula stance by making context-sensitive judgment central.
specificApplications: Identify where a best practice is solving the wrong problem for the current company stage.
Hold accountability and creativity together without pretending the tension disappears.
Use principles to guide judgment instead of replacing it.
commonMisreadings: Treating the chapter as anti-discipline instead of anti-rigidity.
Reading 'no rules' as an excuse to avoid standards or accountability.
hardEdgeRequirement: Hard mode must show why leaders fail when they cling to a rule that solves the wrong context more neatly than the real one.
thresholdQuestion: When does following a clean rule become a way to avoid harder judgment?
